abstract: Introduction IgA1-containing immune complexes (IgA1-IC) consisting of galactose-deficient IgA1 (Gal-deficient IgA1) and IgG autoantibodies are central to the pathogenesis of IgA nephropathy (IgAN). These IgA1-IC form in circulation, and additional proteins may be added before the deposition in the glomeruli. However, the composition of these circulating IgA1-IC is not fully understood. To address this gap in knowledge, we developed a novel proteomic workflow. Methods IgA1-IC from sera of patients with IgAN and healthy controls (HCs) were isolated by lectin-affinity chromatography followed by size-exclusion chromatography (SEC). IgA1 yield and molecular integrity were assessed by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay and sodium dodecyl sulfate–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis. After proteolytic digestion, IgA1-IC samples were analyzed by using liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS). LC-MS results were analyzed by label-free quantification (LFQ) to identify proteins in IgA1-IC of patients with IgAN versus HCs versus proteomes of monomeric IgA1 (mIgA1) and polymeric IgA1 (pIgA1). Results We ascertained that 22 proteins were more abundant in the chromatographic fractions with IgA1-IC from patients with IgAN compared with similar fractions from HCs and other, uncomplexed IgA1 molecular forms. These proteins encompassed immunoglobulins, several complement proteins, including those with regulatory functions, and apolipoproteins. In addition, the identified proteins were validated by use of orthogonal serum preparation and analysis of previously published proteomics data. Conclusion Our new workflow better characterized the serum IgA1-IC of patients with IgAN by identifying proteins with elevated abundance in IgA1-IC in patients with IgAN, including complement components and apolipoproteins. Complement proteins identified in this study indicate that the alternative and lectin pathways are involved, but not the classical pathway.

Isolation of IgA1-IC and Other Molecular Forms of IgA1
To isolate serum IgA1, 500 μl serum and 500 μl calcium-magnesium-free Dulbecco's phosphate-buffered saline (pH: 7.4) were mixed and added to 1 ml packed beads of Dulbecco's phosphate-buffered saline–washed jacalin-agarose (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA). After overnight incubation at 4 °C, bound proteins were eluted with melibiose and concentrated. Concentrated jacalin agarose eluant was then separated using SEC to isolate IgA1-IC and other molecular forms of IgA1 using a calibrated column (Superose 6 Increase 10/300 GL, Sigma-Aldrich) (
Figure 2
). Aliquots of 1 ml fractions from SEC were analyzed by using sodium dodecyl sulfate–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis to identify fractions with IgA1-IC, pIgA1, and mIgA1 molecular forms (
Supplementary Figures S1
and
S2
).

LC-MS Analysis
Chromatographic fractions with IgA1-IC (and other IgA1 molecular forms) were digested with an IgA-specific protease and then trypsin
13
(
Supplementary Figure S3
). Samples were lyophilized and then reconstituted in 0.1% formic acid and loaded onto a reversed-phase C
18
nanocolumn. In
Figure 3

Chromatographic fractions with IgA1-IC from serum samples of 20 patients with IgAN were analyzed using LC-MS on an Orbitrap Velos Pro mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher). High-molecular-mass fractions from sera of HCs corresponding to the size of IgA1-IC in IgAN were negative controls. Proteomes of chromatographic fractions containing pIgA1 and mIgA1 from 20 patients with IgAN and 20 HCs served as additional controls.

Supplementary Methods
. Score-filtered results included relative abundance determined by LFQ of the identified proteins in each sample. Results for proteomes of IgA1-IC, pIgA1, and mIgA1 are in
Supplementary Data S3
to
S5
, respectively. Mass spectrometry data were deposited to the ProteomeXchange Consortium via the PRIDE
14
partner repository with dataset identifier PXD055562 and 10.6019/PXD055562.
Qualitative and quantitative comparisons of proteins identified in chromatographic fractions with different molecular forms of IgA1 were performed using Scaffold perSPECtives (version 3.1.0, Proteome Software; workflow in
Supplementary Figure S5

Supplementary Data S3–S5

Figure 4
a and
Supplementary Figure S4

Figure 4
c,

Orthogonal Validation of Proteome of Chromatographic Fractions with IgA1-IC
As an orthogonal means of confirming IgA1-IC proteins, we used chromatographic fractions with IgA1-IC from native serum of a patient with IgAN and corresponding fractions from the same serum that was IgA-depleted. IgA was depleted using CNBr-activated Sepharose beads with covalently linked goat antihuman IgA antibody. The resultant samples were analyzed by using LC-MS and processed as described above. Relative protein abundance was assessed using LFQ and the abundance ratio was calculated for samples from native serum versus IgA-depleted serum. All proteins compared in this analysis are listed in
Supplementary Data S7
, including a curated list of proteins identified as absent (i.e., below the level of detection) or depleted > 2-fold in IgA-depleted versus native-serum samples. These proteins were compared with those identified in the proteomes of IgA1-IC and are marked in
Table 2
(last column). Detailed methods are provided in the
Supplementary Methods
.
body:
IgA nephropathy (IgAN) is a common primary glomerulonephritis. Most patients progress to kidney failure in their lifetime.
1
,
2
IgAN is characterized by IgA1-containing immunodeposits in the glomeruli that, based on immunofluorescence microscopy, include variable amounts of IgG and IgM and usually with complement C3 but not C1q, suggestive of involvement of the alternative but not classical complement pathway.
1
,
3
,
4
Co-deposits of complement proteins of the lectin pathway are detected in approximately 25% to 30% of patients and are associated with worse disease progression.
5
,
6
Current understanding of the pathogenesis of IgAN is described by a 4-hit hypothesis (
Figure 1
). IgA1 contains a hinge region with 3-6
O
-glycans. Most patients with IgAN have elevated circulatory levels of IgA1 with some of those
O
-glycans deficient in galactose (Gal-deficient IgA1) (Hit #1). This Gal-deficient IgA1 is recognized by autoantibodies (Hit #2) to form circulating immune complexes (IgA1-IC) with additional blood proteins added (Hit #3). Some of these complexes deposit in glomeruli, activate mesangial cells, and induce kidney injury (Hit #4).
1
,
7
Figure 1
Four-hit hypothesis for the pathogenesis of IgA nephropathy (IgAN). The pathogenesis of IgAN can be described by a multihit mechanism. In the blood of most patients with IgAN, there is an elevated level of galactose (Gal)-deficient IgA (Hit #1). The Gal-deficient-IgA1 is recognized by IgG autoantibodies (Hit #2). The resultant immune complexes can have additional proteins added to form pathogenic IgA1-containing immune complexes (IgA1-IC) in the circulation (Hit #3). Some of these IgA1-IC deposit in glomeruli to induce kidney injury (Hit #4). Created with
BioRender.com
.
This hypothesis is supported by multiple clinical and laboratory findings. Glomerular immunodeposits in IgAN are enriched for Gal-deficient IgA1
8
,
9
and IgG autoantibodies specific for Gal-deficient IgA1.
1
,
4
,
8
Experiments based on serum depleted of IgA1, serum supplemented with Gal-deficient IgA1, serum supplemented with immune complexes formed from Gal-deficient IgA1 and IgG autoantibodies, and a passive mouse model of IgAN confirm the nephritogenic properties of IgA1-IC.
10
,
11
,
12
These complexes in the circulation of patients with IgAN have a high molecular mass (> 700 kDa),
10
presumably because of the presence of additional proteins, such as complement C3. The amount of IgA1 in IgA1-IC represents a very small fraction (< 0.1%) of total serum IgA1; thus, IgA1-IC are difficult to analyze by routine protocols.
In this study, we developed a proteomic workflow to characterize the composition of IgA1-IC in IgAN. This workflow is based on the isolation of total serum IgA1 by lectin-affinity chromatography followed by size-exclusion chromatography (SEC) to separate IgA1-IC from the other 2 molecular forms of IgA1, monomeric IgA1 (mIgA1) and polymeric IgA1 (pIgA1). Using this workflow, we prepared chromatographic fractions containing IgA1-IC from serum samples of 20 patients with IgAN and the corresponding high-molecular-mass fractions from sera of 20 healthy controls (HCs). Proteomes of these samples were analyzed using high-resolution LC-MS. Our new workflow enabled targeted identification of proteins with elevated abundance in IgA1-IC of patients with IgAN. These results provide new targets to be evaluated for their roles in the formation and activity of nephritogenic IgA1-IC in IgAN.

Identification of the Proteomes of Chromatographic Fractions with IgA1-IC in IgAN
Using our novel serum proteomics strategy, we profiled chromatographic fractions with IgA1-IC from 20 patients with IgAN and the corresponding fractions from 20 HCs (
Figure 4
a–d). Proteomes of pIgA1 and mIgA1 were analyzed for comparison. Immunoglobulins
The IgA1-IC fractions included 5 Ig component chains, namely IgA1 heavy chain, κ and λ light chains, J chain, and IgM heavy chain. These Ig chains had higher abundance (
P
< 0.001) in the IgA1-IC from patients with IgAN versus the chromatographic fractions of the same molecular mass from HCs. Two variable-region segments, Ig heavy-chain variable segment 5-10-1 and Ig lambda-chain variable segment 1-47, were in only the IgA1-IC combined dataset from patients with IgAN (
Supplementary Data S5
). The difference in abundance between constant regions and variable regions of Igs in the IgA1-IC was like that in the chromatographic fractions with mIgA1, indicating no enrichment for specific variable segments of Igs in the IgA1-IC. Notably, only low levels of IgG heavy chain were identified in the IgA1-IC fractions. Based on our previous isolation of IgA1-IC, we hypothesized that our 2-step protocol may have disrupted the IgA1-IC and led to loss of IgG before LC-MS.
Proteins Associated with the Complement System
Complement-associated proteins with a >2-fold greater abundance in IgA1-IC fractions from patients with IgAN versus the same corresponding fractions from HCs included C4b-binding protein α chain (

< 0.0048), complement C4-A/B (

Next, we evaluated the data in the context of the complement-activation pathways (classical, lectin, and alternative) and their regulatory components.
C3 is processed by a proteolytic cleavage during activation and additional cleavage is associated with its inactivation. Although IgA1-IC proteomic analysis did not allow distinction between different C3 cleavage fragments, by examining the sequence coverage and relative abundance of C3 in our analysis of the pooled IgAN-patient samples, we hypothesized that we could find indications of C3 cleavage products. We generated an amino-acid sequence map of complement C3 which includes the α- and β-subunits,
17
and downstream cleavage products, C3a, C3b, C3f, inactivated C3b (iC3b), C3dg, and C3d

; some samples may also have C3b and iC3b in varying amounts and ratios.
18
C4 can be involved in the lectin or classical pathway of complement and is regulated by C4b-binding protein a chain a cofactor for C3b/C4b inactivator (i.e., complement factor I). For the classical complement pathway, tryptic peptides from several components (complement C1q, C1r, and C1s,) were identified (

Supplementary Data S5

Our bioinformatics analyses indicated that the IgA1-IC proteomes in patients with IgAN had elevated amounts of some proteins from the alternative complement pathway, and possibly lectin pathway, whereas the proteins from the classical pathway were not significantly involved. The IgAN IgA1-IC fractions had also complement-regulating proteins, such as clusterin and C4b-binding protein α chain.
Apolipoproteins
Nine different apolipoproteins were identified in chromatographic fractions with IgA1-IC from patients with IgAN. Except for apolipoprotein A-1, these components had a ≥2-fold relative abundance in IgAN-derived IgA1-IC compared with corresponding fractions from HCs (
Table 2
), with the highest being that of apolipoprotein C-IV. Although apolipoprotein (a) had only 10% sequence coverage (58 exclusively unique peptides), the protein itself is large (4568 amino acids) and, thus, we consider the coverage significant.

Orthogonal Analysis of IgA1-IC
To test the hypothesis that our 2-step protocol disrupted IgA1-IC leading to the loss of IgG in our LC-MS analysis, we used chromatographic fractions with IgA1-IC from native serum of a patient with IgAN and corresponding fractions from the sera of 2 patients with IgAN, that were IgA-depleted. IgA1-IC from a patient with IgAN were isolated using SEC and fractions > 700 kDa were pooled. Equivalent high-molecular-mass fractions from the IgA-depleted serum samples served as a control. LC-MS identified 131 proteins in the > 700 kDa fractions of IgA1-IC (
Supplementary Data S7
). IgA depletion removed IgA1 and IgA2 and removed or reduced 32 other Ig-derived polypeptides from the IgA1-IC fractions of native serum. Significantly, IgG heavy chain was clearly present at levels comparable to those for IgA1 in the > 700 kDa fractions of native serum. In the 2 IgA-depleted serum samples, IgG was not detected, indicating that it was depleted along with the IgA. This finding indicated that our 2-step protocol had influenced the amount of IgG in the high-molecular-mass fractions.
Of the 131 proteins identified in IgA1-IC from native serum, 36 were not detected in the IgA-depleted samples and the amounts of 22 other proteins were reduced >2-fold (58 total,
Supplementary Data S7
). Of the 22 highly abundant proteins in IgA1-IC of patients with IgAN in our initial analysis (
Table 2
), 12 were removed or reduced after IgA depletion of serum. These proteins included Ig component chains (IgA1 heavy chain, κ light chain, and J chain), 5 complement-associated proteins, 3 apolipoproteins, and fibronectin (
Table 2
). The results provide corroborating evidence that the directly identified IgA1-IC proteins from patients with IgAN compared with the same corresponding fractions from HCs were significant. Interestingly, most of the apolipoproteins and IgM were not depleted, indicating they may represent a distinct high-molecular-mass complex not associated with IgA1-IC, given that IgM binds low-density lipoproteins.
19
To further evaluate our data, we compared our results with those from a previous transcriptomic and proteomic study.
20
This study focused on serum preparations of IgA1 from patients with IgAN that were incubated with serum-starved mesangial cells and the cells then underwent transcriptomic and proteomic analyses. Based on our analysis of publicly available proteomic results, several identified proteins were enriched in the mesangial cells incubated with preparations of IgA1 (that included IgA-IC) relative to control cells. These proteins likely originated from the serum IgA preparations, because transcriptomic analyses detected no or only low levels of expression by mesangial cells. Several of these enriched proteins overlapped with our identifications, thus further validating our results. Details of our bioinformatic comparison between this study and our study are provided in

Discussion
This is the first study to comprehensively analyze proteins in IgA1-IC in the circulation of patients with IgAN. The proteome analysis used IgA1-IC isolated from sera of patients with IgAN and series of corresponding fractions from sera of HCs by lectin-affinity chromatography combined with SEC. Our novel relative-quantitative proteomics analysis identified 22 proteins with significantly higher abundance in IgA1-IC fractions from patients with IgAN than background levels of high-molecular-mass proteins in the comparable fractions from HCs.
Incomplete information about the composition of IgA1-IC has been a major gap in understanding the pathogenesis and clinical expression of IgAN. Several studies have reported proteomics analyses of urine and immunodeposits in the kidneys, whereas other studies attempted to assess the composition of immune complexes using whole-serum samples.
21
,
22
,
23
,
24
These approaches are challenging because of the complexity of samples wherein hundreds of proteins are identified in a single run without clarity as to which are associated with IgA1-IC.
Multiple studies have shown that IgA1-IC in the circulation of patients with IgAN are of large molecular mass (> 700 kDa), contain Gal-deficient IgA1 (Gd-IgA1) and anti-Gd-IgA1 IgG autoantibodies, activate primary human mesangial cells in culture,
3
,
7
,
25
,
26
,
27
and can be removed from serum samples by using immobilized jacalin to bind IgA1.
10
,
12
Jacalin-agarose binds
O
-glycosylated proteins. The goal was to isolate high molecular mass IgAN-related immune complexes from patients with IgAN while comparing an equivalent fraction from healthy individuals. Our chosen methodology had the potential to isolate other serum
O
-glycosylated proteins that were part of high molecular mass fraction and potentially not associated with the IgA1-IC. We have made note of these proteins in
Table 2
. Importantly, by comparing equivalent fractions from HC volunteers, we establish which proteins are likely to comprise the background and are not quantitatively enriched compared with those we are reporting from the patients with IgAN. Furthermore, jacalin-isolated IgA1-IC from patients with IgAN activate cultured primary human mesangial cells more than do jacalin-isolated IgA1-IC from HCs.
20
Based on these published results, we developed our 2-step chromatography protocol to isolate IgA1-IC for targeted proteomic and bioinformatic analyses separate from the main IgA1 molecular forms in serum, mIgA1 and pIgA1. This approach increased the likelihood that the identified proteins are associated with nephritogenic IgA1-IC.
Constant-region segments of the heavy chain of IgA1 and of Ig light chains were among the most abundant proteins identified in IgA1-IC. Variable-region segments of Ig heavy and light chains exhibited an order-of-magnitude lower abundance. This finding mimicked the pattern of abundance for Ig variable and constant regions in chromatographic fractions with mIgA1, indicating that IgA1 antibodies in the IgA1-IC are likely polyclonal without an enrichment for clonotypes with specific variable-region segments.
We detected lower levels of IgG heavy chain constant-region segments than expected in the chromatographic fraction with IgA1-IC from patients with IgAN. The results from our analysis of IgA-depleted serum showed IgG at levels equivalent to IgA1 in IgA1-IC fractions from sera of patients with IgAN. Both IgA and IgG were subsequently depleted (via IgA-specific antibody) from the serum before SEC. In addition, several other proteins, including C3, were depleted from the high-molecular-weight fractions. Importantly, there was extensive overlap in the proteins identified by the 2 distinct preparations we used in our study. This finding indicates that the 2-step isolation disrupted the autoantibody-antigen interaction, consistent with the 1-step IgA depletion that demonstrated a codepletion of IgG with IgA. In other studies, we have confirmed the association of IgA1 and IgG in IgA1-IC in patients with IgAN (Hall et al., 2023).
Our findings are supported by results of a previous proteomic study of mesangial cells incubated with lectin-isolated IgA1 from sera of patients with IgAN.
20
The proteome of IgA1-supplemented mesangial cells included proteins not expressed by the mesangial cells that likely originated from IgA1-IC. Several of those proteins were identified in our direct assessment of IgA1-IC from patients with IgAN. Although not directly addressed in the paper,
20
we hypothesize that these proteins originated from the IgA1-IC, thus further validating our current results and providing new insight into the previous study. These data represent 3 unique preparations of serum IgA1-associated proteins that show a common set of protein identifications that likely represent the core of nephritogenic immune complexes.
In agreement with other studies, our results indicate an extensive involvement of the complement system in IgA1-IC. In fact, the complement-related proteins we identified were at levels of equal abundance as IgA. The observed tryptic fragments were derived from α and β chains of C3. The presence of C3a is consistent with intact α chain of C3 in IgA1-IC,
5
although C3b and iC3b may also be present (Hall et al., 2023). Importantly, our serum proteomic analysis supports the inclusion of C3 within circulating IgA1-IC before glomerular deposition, consistent with C3 being covalently associated with IgA1-IC.
18
Several other complement-associated proteins were identified, including complement C4, C4b-binding protein α chain, clusterin, and vitamin K–dependent protein S. C4 can be involved in the lectin or classical pathway of complement activation, because C4b participates in formation of C3 convertase (C4bC2a complex). C4 is regulated by C4b-binding protein α chain that is a cofactor for C3b/C4b inactivator (i.e., complement factor I). C4b-binding protein also accelerates degradation of the C4bC2a complex by dissociating the complement fragment C2a, with the α chain binding C4b. C4b-binding protein α chain also binds anticoagulant protein S. Notably, free but not complexed protein S has anticoagulant activity and can serve as a cofactor to protein C to inactivate coagulation factors Va and VIIIa. Another complement-associated protein, clusterin, is a heterodimeric multifunctional protein that forms high-density lipid complexes in blood and participates in control of the lytic activity of the terminal complement complex.
28
Complement C1q, C1r, and C1s proteins were observed at low levels in IgA1-IC fractions from patients with IgAN and at equivalent levels in IgA1-IC fractions from HCs. This finding indicates a lesser role, if any, for involvement of the classical pathway of complement in formation of the IgA1-IC. Identification of other proteins, such as mannose-binding lectin and ficolins 2 and 3, in only a subset of sera from patients with IgAN and none from HCs, demonstrates heterogeneity in IgA1-IC across patients. This finding is consistent with the observed heterogeneity of size and activity of IgA1-IC, as we and others have published.
10
,
12
Large IgA1-IC enhance proliferation of mesangial cells in culture; whereas, in some patients, smaller IgA1-IC inhibit cellular proliferation.
12
Furthermore, the amount, size, and activity of IgA1-IC vary at disease activity versus disease quiescence.
10
,
29
Different complexes may exhibit different sizes and compositions and contain; in addition to IgA1, only a subset of proteins that we identified in IgA1-IC in patients with IgAN. Continued development of proteomic strategies focused on serum IgA1-IC will allow a more precise determination of the heterogeneity of IgA1-IC at the molecular level.
We identified 9 apolipoproteins enriched in the IgA1-IC fractions in patients with IgAN. Currently, apolipoproteins have not been assessed for a potential role in the pathogenesis of IgAN. Studies have suggested that apolipoproteins are associated with the phenotype of IgAN and severity of glomerular injury, based on protective (e.g., apolipoprotein M
30
) or damaging (e.g., apolipoprotein E
31
) effects. Furthermore, apolipoproteins (A1, B, and E) have been implicated in progression of chronic kidney disease.
31
,
32
,
33
,
34
,
35
We observed a high abundance of apolipoprotein B in IgAN IgA1-IC. Apolipoprotein C-III, another protein that was enriched in IgA1-IC in patients with IgAN, has been associated with high serum triglyceride levels in patients with chronic kidney disease.
36
Apolipoproteins can self-aggregate and form larger complexes. It is possible that their presence in the IgA1-IC fractions from patients with IgAN is independent of the nephritogenic immune complexes. Only 3 of the 9 apolipoproteins (A-1, B, and [a]) were reduced or depleted in the single analysis of IgA-depleted serum.
There were some limitations to this study of isolated serum IgA1-IC in IgAN. This biopsy-proven IgAN cohort was representative of patients with IgAN from early-stage disease to advanced chronic kidney disease, which can be seen in the wide range of clinical values collected in
Table 1
and
Supplementary Data S1-S2
. Specifically, 3 of the patients sampled were experiencing kidney failure and were on dialysis, and yet their identified abundant proteins in the high molecular-mass serum fractions were consistent with the remaining samples. Future studies that subdivide patients with early- and late-stage IgAN may provide more insight into the nature of immune complexes.
In summary, we developed a novel proteomic workflow to analyze composition of circulating IgA1-IC in IgAN. This workflow identified 22 proteins that were more abundant in IgA1-IC fractions of serum of patients with IgAN than in those of HCs. These proteins included IgA1 of polyclonal origin, complement components, and apolipoproteins. We confirmed our findings by orthogonal validation experiments and bioinformatic analysis of previously published proteomic data. Our results provide new targets to be evaluated for their roles in the formation and activity of nephritogenic IgA1-IC in IgAN. Future studies will determine whether some targets provide a basis for identification of patients at risk of progressive loss of kidney function.
